notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0159.stoa004.opp-la: In 18 the printed *eiectorum* is read as *electorum*, 'of the elect'. Section 26 breaks off at 'Belial...' in this edition.

In 100 the printed *miles* is read as *mites*, 'gentle'; the clause *mites sunt immanibus* is awkward as printed and is rendered by its evident sense, that *Manes* is the opposite of *immanes*. *Ficarius* (104) is left in Latin; it seems to come from *ficus*, 'fig'. The Horace line is translated as printed here (*incedis*, 'you pass').
The third section is printed '85'; it is 83. In 85 the printed *eam* is read as *eum*, 'him'.

nodes.text: 1. There is some difference between astronomy and astrology. For astronomy covers the revolution of the heavens and the risings, settings and motions of the stars, and why they are so called. Astrology, however, is partly natural, partly superstitious.

2. It is natural when it follows the courses of the sun and moon, or of the stars, and the fixed stations of the seasons. But the superstitious [kind] is the one the *mathematici* [astrologers] follow, who take auguries in the stars, who also distribute the twelve signs over the individual members of the soul or body, and who try to predict people's nativities and characters from the course of the stars.

1. They are called angels (*angeli*) in Greek; in Hebrew they are called *melachim*; in Latin they are rendered *nuntii*, 'messengers', from the fact that they announce (*nuntient*) the will of the Lord to the peoples.
2. The word 'angel', however, is the name of an office, not of a nature; for they are always spirits, but when they are sent they are called angels.

3. Painters' licence gives them wings for this reason, to signify their swift movement to every place, just as, in the tales of the poets, the winds too are said to have wings, that is, because of their speed. Hence Holy Scripture says: 'Who walks upon the wings of the winds' (Ps. CIII, 5).

4. The holy Scriptures testify that there are nine orders of angels, that is: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim and seraphim; and by interpreting them we shall set out why the names of these offices are so given.
5. They are called angels because they are sent from heaven to bring announcements to human beings; for what is *angelus* in Greek is called *nuntius*, 'messenger', in Latin.

6. Archangels, [a word] in the Greek language, are rendered in Latin 'highest messengers'; for those who announce small or very small things are called angels, but those who announce the highest things, archangels. They are called archangels because they hold first place among the angels; for Greek *archos* is rendered in Latin *princeps*, 'chief'. For they are leaders and chiefs, under whose ordering the duties of each of the angels are assigned.

7. For that archangels are set over angels the prophet Zechariah testifies, saying: 'And behold, the angel who spoke in me went out, and another angel went out to meet him, and said to him: Run, speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall' (Zac. II, 3).
8. For if, in the very duties of the angels, the higher powers did not direct the lower, the angel would in no way have learned from an angel what he was to say to the man.
9. Some of the archangels are called by personal names, so that by the names themselves it may be indicated what they can do in their work.
10. Gabriel is turned from Hebrew into our language as 'strength of God'. For where divine power or strength is made manifest, Gabriel is sent.
11. Hence too, at the time when the Lord was to be born and to triumph over the world, Gabriel came to Mary to announce him who deigned to come in humility to vanquish the powers of the air.

12. Michael is interpreted 'Who is like God?' For when something of wondrous power is done in the world, this archangel is sent. And his name comes from the work itself, because no one can do what God is able to do.
13. Raphael is interpreted 'healing' or 'medicine of God'; for wherever a work of curing and healing is needed, this archangel is sent by God, and from this he is called the medicine of God.
14. Hence the same archangel, sent to Tobias, applied a cure to his eyes and, wiping away the blindness, restored his sight; for by the interpretation of the name the angel's office too is indicated.
15. Uriel is interpreted 'Fire of God', as we read that fire appeared in the bush. We read also that fire was sent from above and fulfilled what had been commanded.

16. Thrones, and dominions, and principalities, and powers, and virtues, by which [names] the Apostle encompasses the whole heavenly society, are understood as orders and ranks of angels; and according to this very distribution of offices some are called thrones, some dominions, some principalities, some powers, according to the fixed ranks by which they are distinguished from one another.
17. The virtues (*virtutes*, 'powers' or 'mighty works') are said to be certain angelic ministries through which signs and miracles are done in the world, which is why they are called virtues.

18. The powers (*potestates*) are those to whom the hostile virtues are subject, and they are called by the name of powers because the malign spirits are restrained by their power, so that they may not harm the world as much as they desire.

19. The principalities are those who are set over the hosts of angels. Because they direct the angels under them to fulfil the divine ministry, they received the name of principalities. For some are those who minister, others those who stand by, as is said through Daniel: 'Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him' (Dan. VII, 10).
20. The dominions are those who are pre-eminent even over the virtues and principalities; because they hold dominion over the other hosts of angels, they are called dominions.
21. The thrones are hosts of angels who in Latin speech are called *sedes*, 'seats'; and they are called thrones because the Creator presides over them and through them disposes his judgements.

22. The cherubim, too, are said to be exalted powers of the heavens and angelic ministries; they are interpreted from Hebrew into our language as 'multitude of knowledge'. For they are the more exalted hosts of angels who, because they are placed nearer [to God] and are filled with divine knowledge more fully than the rest, are called cherubim, that is, 'fullness of knowledge'.
23. They are those two creatures fashioned from metal above the mercy seat of the Ark, to signify the presence of angels, in whose midst God is shown.

24. The seraphim, likewise, are a multitude of angels, who are interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as 'burning' or 'kindling'; they are called burning because no angels stand between them and God, and so, the nearer they stand before him, the more they are set aflame by the brightness of the divine light.
25. Hence they also veil the face and feet of God sitting on the throne, and therefore the rest of the throng of angels cannot fully see the essence of God, since the seraphim cover it.

26. These names of the hosts of angels, then, are particular to the individual orders in such a way that they are nevertheless in part common to all. For while the thrones, the seats of God, are specifically designated in the order of certain angels, yet through the Psalmist it is said: 'You who sit upon the cherubim' (Ps. LXXIX, 2).

27. But these orders of angels are called by their own names because each received this very office more fully in its own order. And although they are common to all, these names are nevertheless assigned as proper to their own orders.

28. For to each, as was said before, its own duties have been assigned, which it is agreed they earned at the beginning of the world. For that angels preside over both places and people, an angel testifies through the prophet, saying: 'The prince of the kingdom of the Persians withstood me' (Dan. x, 13).
29. From this it is plain that there is no place over which angels do not preside. For they also preside over the beginnings of all undertakings.

3. And so this vanity of the magic arts, from the teaching of the evil angels, held sway throughout the whole world for very many ages, through a certain knowledge of the future and through summonings of those below. Their inventions are haruspicy, augury, the so-called oracles themselves, and necromancy.

9. *Magi*, magicians, are those who are commonly called *malefici*, evildoers, because of the magnitude of their crimes (*facinora*). They shake the elements, disturb people's minds, and without any draught of poison they kill by the sheer violence of a spell.

11. Necromancers are those by whose incantations the dead, brought back to life, seem to prophesy and to answer what they are asked. For in Greek *nekros* means 'dead' and *manteia* 'divination'; to question them, blood is added to the corpse, for they say that demons love blood; and so whenever necromancy is performed, gore is mixed with water, so that they may be more easily called forth by the colour of blood.

28. Lot-casters (*sortilegi*) are those who, under the name of a pretended religion, profess a science of divination by certain [lots] which they call 'the lots of the saints', or who promise [to reveal] the future by inspecting any writings whatever.

30. To all these belong also the *ligaturae* [bound amulets] of accursed remedies, which the art of physicians condemns, whether in incantations, or in written characters, or in any things whatever that are hung or tied on.
33. Mercury is said to have been the first to invent illusion (*praestigium*). It is called *praestigium* because it dims (*praestingat*) the eyes' sight.

1. Those whom the pagans claim as gods are reported to have once been human beings, and according to the life or merits of each they began to be worshipped among their own people after death, as Isis in Egypt, Jupiter in Crete, Juba among the Moors, Faunus among the Latins, Quirinus among the Romans.

2. In the same way too, Minerva at Athens, Juno on Samos, Venus at Paphos, Vulcan on Lemnos, Liber on Naxos, Apollo at Delphi; and the poets also joined in their praises and, by composing songs, raised them up to heaven.

3. For the inventions of certain arts are said to have brought forth [their] worship, as medicine for Aesculapius, smithing for Vulcan. They are also named from their activities, as Mercury, because he presides over merchandise (*merces*); Liber from freedom (*libertas*).

4. There were also certain brave men, or founders of cities, for whom, when they died, the people who loved them fashioned images, so that they might have some comfort from contemplating the likenesses; but little by little, at the persuasion of demons, this error is known to have crept in among later generations, so that those whom the former had honoured only for the remembrance of their name, their successors considered gods and worshipped.

5. The use of images arose when, out of longing for the dead, images or effigies were set up, as if for those received into heaven; in their place demons put themselves forward on earth to be worshipped, and persuaded the deceived and the lost to sacrifice to them.

15. They say that demons were named by the Greeks as if *daēmones*, that is, experienced and knowing about things. For they know many future things in advance, which is why they are also accustomed to give certain responses.

16. For there is in them a knowledge of things greater than human weakness has, partly through the sharpness of a subtler perception, partly through the experience of a very long life, partly through angelic revelation at God's command. They flourish with the nature of airy bodies.

17. Before the transgression, indeed, they bore heavenly bodies. But when they fell they were changed into an airy quality, and they were permitted to hold not the purer regions of that air but these murky ones, [this air] being as it were a prison for them until the time of judgement. These are the transgressing angels, whose prince is the devil.

18. *Diabolus* [devil] in Hebrew is said to mean 'flowing downward', because he scorned to stand at rest on the summit of heaven, but, plunging downward under the weight of pride, he fell. In Greek, however, *diabolus* means *criminator*, 'accuser', either because he reports to God the crimes into which he himself entices [people], or because he accuses the innocence of the elect with invented crimes; hence in the Apocalypse it is said by an angelic voice: 'The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them in the sight of our God day and night.'

19. *Satanas* [Satan] in Latin means 'adversary' or 'transgressor'. For he is the adversary, since he is the enemy of truth and always strives to oppose the virtues of the saints; he is also the transgressor, because, having turned transgressor, he did not stand in the truth in which he was created; he is likewise the tempter, because he asks that the innocence of the just be put to the test, as is written in Job.

20. He is called Antichrist because he is to come against Christ. Not as some simple people understand it, that he is called Antichrist because he is to come before (*ante*) Christ, that is, that Christ will come after him; not so, but *Antichristus* is said in Greek, which in Latin is 'contrary to Christ'; for Greek *anti* means *contra*, 'against', in Latin.
21. For when he comes he will falsely claim to be Christ, and he will fight against him, and he will oppose the sacraments of Christ, in order to destroy the Gospel of his truth.

22. For he will also attempt to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem and to restore all the ceremonies of the old law. But he too is Antichrist who denies that Christ is God, for he is contrary to Christ; for all who go out from the Church and are cut off from the unity of the faith are themselves antichrists too.

23. Bel is a Babylonian idol, [a name] which is interpreted 'old'; for this Belus, the father of Ninus, was the first king of the Assyrians, and some call him Saturn. This name was later venerated both among the Assyrians and among the Africans, whence in the Punic language god is called *Bal*. Among the Assyrians, however, by a certain reckoning of their rites, both Saturn and the Sun are called Bel.
24. Beelphegor is interpreted 'image of shame'; for it was the idol of Moab, surnamed Baal, on Mount Phegor, whom the Latins call Priapus, god of gardens.

25. For he came from Lampsacus, a city of the Hellespont, from which he was driven out; and because of the size of his male member the Greeks transferred him into the number of their gods and consecrated him as the divinity of gardens; hence he is also said to preside over gardens, because of their fertility.

26. Beelzebub was the idol of Ekron, which is interpreted 'man of flies'; for a fly is called *zebub*. This most filthy idol, then, is called 'man of flies' because of the filth of idolatry, or because of its uncleanness. Belial...

27. Behemoth, from a Hebrew word, means 'animal' in the Latin language, because he fell from the heights to earthly things and for his deserts was made like a brute animal. He is also Leviathan, that is, 'serpent from the waters', because in the sea of this world he moves about with twisting cunning.

28. Leviathan, moreover, is interpreted 'their addition'—that is, of none other than human beings, on whom he once brought the guilt of transgression in paradise, and this [guilt] he daily adds to, or extends, by persuasion, as far as eternal death.

49. He is called Hermes in Greek from *hermēneia*, 'interpretation'; in Latin, *interpres*, 'interpreter'. On account of his excellence and his knowledge of many arts he was named Trismegistus, that is, 'thrice greatest'. When they represent him with a dog's head, the reason given is that among all animals the dog is held to be the most keen-scented and sharp-sighted kind.

73. On her breast the Gorgon's head is represented for this reason, that all wisdom is there, which confounds others and proves them ignorant and stony; this we also see on ancient statues of emperors, in the middle of the breast of the cuirass, to suggest wisdom and valour.

81. The Greeks say Pan, the Latins Silvanus: the god of country people, whom they shaped in the likeness of nature; hence he is called Pan, that is, 'all'. For they represent him as made from the universal form of the elements.

82. For he has horns in the likeness of the rays of the Sun and Moon. He has a skin marked with spots, for the stars of the sky. His face is red, in the likeness of the aether. He carries a pipe of seven reeds, for the harmony of heaven, in which there are seven sounds and seven distinctions of notes.

83. He is shaggy, because the earth is clothed over and shaken by the winds. His lower part is ugly, because of the trees and wild beasts and herds. He has goats' hooves, to show the solidity of the earth, he whom they make the god of things and of all nature; hence they say Pan, as if 'all things'.

84. Isis in the language of the Egyptians is called 'earth', which they hold to be Isis. Now Isis was a queen of the Egyptians, the daughter of King Inachus, who, coming from Greece, taught the Egyptians letters and established the tilling of the land; for this reason they also called the earth by her name.

85. Serapis is the greatest of all the gods of the Egyptians. He is Apis, king of the Argives, who was carried by ship to Egypt and, when he had died there, was called Serapis, for this reason: because the chest in which a dead person is placed, which they call a sarcophagus, is called *soros* in Greek, and there they began to venerate him, buried [in it], before his temple was built; as if *soros* [and] Apis, he was called first *Sorapis* and then, with a letter changed, Serapis.

100. They say that the *Manes* are the gods of the dead, whose power, they claim, lies between the moon and the earth; from them they think *mane*, 'morning', was named. They think they were called *Manes* from the air, which is *manus*, that is, thin, or because they flow (*manant*) widely through the breezes; or else, because they are gentle (*mites*), they are called by this name, the contrary of *immanes*, 'monstrous'. Apuleius, however, says that they are called *Manes* by antiphrasis (*kat' antiphrasin*), that is, 'gentle' and 'mild', though they are terrible and monstrous, like the Parcae and the Eumenides.
101. They say that *larvae* [ghosts] are demons made from human beings who were of evil desert. Their nature is said to be to frighten little children and to chatter in dark corners.
102. *Lamiae*, who stories say used to seize infants and tear them apart, are named specifically from tearing (*laniando*).

103. The 'hairy ones' (*pilosi*), who are called *Panitae* in Greek and *Incubi* in Latin; or *Inui*, from their mating (*ineundo*) indiscriminately with animals; whence they are also called *Incubi*, from lying upon (*incumbendo*), that is, ravishing. For they often show themselves lewd even toward women and achieve intercourse with them; the Gauls call these demons *Dusii*, because they constantly commit this uncleanness.
104. The one whom people commonly call *Incubo*, the Romans call Faunus *Ficarius*; to him Horace says: 'Faunus, lover of the fleeing Nymphs, through my lands and sunny fields you pass gently.'
